9.1: He who acts unjustly acts impiously. For since the universal nature has made rational animals for the sake of one another, to help one another according to their deserts, but in no way to harm one another, he who breaks her will is clearly guilty of impiety towards the highest divinity. And he too who lies is guilty of impiety to the same divinity; for the universal nature is the nature of things that are, and things that are have a relation to all things that come into existence. And further, this universal nature is called truth, and is the first cause of all things that are true. He, then, who lies intentionally is guilty of impiety, in that he acts unjustly by deceiving; and so is he who lies unintentionally, in that he is at odds with the universal nature, and in that he disturbs the order by fighting against the nature of the world; for he fights against it who is moved of his own accord towards what is contrary to truth, for he had received powers from nature, through neglecting which he is now unable to distinguish falsehood from truth. And indeed he who pursues pleasure as good, and avoids pain as evil, is guilty of impiety. For such a man must necessarily often find fault with the universal nature, claiming that it assigns things to the bad and the good contrary to their deserts, because the bad often enjoy pleasure and possess the things which produce pleasure, while the good have pain as their share, and the things which cause pain. And further, he who is afraid of pain will sometimes also be afraid of some of the things which will happen in the world, and even this is impiety. And he who pursues pleasure will not keep from injustice, and this is plainly impiety. Now with respect to the things towards which the universal nature is equally disposed—for it would not have made both unless it were equally disposed towards both—towards these, those who wish to follow nature should be of the same mind with it, and equally disposed. With respect to pain, then, and pleasure, or death and life, or honour and dishonour, which the universal nature uses equally, whoever is not equally disposed towards them is clearly acting impiously. And I say that the universal nature uses them equally, instead of saying that they happen alike to those who are produced in continuous succession and to those who come after them, by virtue of a certain original movement of Providence, by which it moved from a certain beginning to this ordering of things, having conceived certain principles of the things that were to be, and having determined powers that produce beings and changes and such successions.
9.2: It would be a man's happiest lot to leave mankind without having had any taste of lying and hypocrisy and luxury and pride. However, to breathe out one's life when a man has had enough of these things is the next best voyage, as the saying goes. Have you decided to stay with vice, and has experience not yet persuaded you to flee from this plague? For the destruction of the understanding is a plague, much more, indeed, than any such corruption and change of the air which surrounds us. For this corruption is a plague of animals in so far as they are animals; but the other is a plague of men in so far as they are men.
9.3: Do not despise death, but be well content with it, since this too is one of those things which nature wills. For just as it is to be young and to grow old, and to grow and to reach maturity, and to have teeth and beard and grey hairs, and to father children and to be pregnant and to give birth, and all the other natural processes which the seasons of your life bring, so too is dissolution. This, then, is in keeping with the character of a thoughtful man—to be neither careless nor impatient nor contemptuous with regard to death, but to wait for it as one of the processes of nature. As you now wait for the time when the child shall come out of your wife's womb, so be ready for the time when your soul shall fall out of this covering. But if you also want a common kind of comfort which will reach your heart, you will be best reconciled to death by observing the things from which you are going to be removed, and the morals of those with whom your soul will no longer be mingled. For it is in no way right to be offended with men, but it is your duty to care for them and to bear with them gently; and yet to remember that your departure will not be from men who have the same principles as yourself. For this is the only thing, if there is any, which could pull us the other way and attach us to life—to be allowed to live with those who have the same principles as ourselves. But as it is, you see how great is the trouble arising from the discord of those who live together, so that you may say: Come quickly, O death, in case I too should forget myself.
9.4: He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
9.5: He often acts unjustly who does not do a certain thing; not only he who does a certain thing.
9.6: Your present opinion founded on understanding, and your present conduct directed to the social good, and your present disposition of contentment with everything which happens—that is enough.
9.7: Wipe out imagination; check desire; extinguish appetite; keep the ruling faculty in its own power.
9.8: Among the animals which do not have reason, one life is distributed; but among reasonable animals, one intelligent soul is distributed: just as there is one earth for all things which are of an earthly nature, and we see by one light, and breathe one air, all of us that have the faculty of sight and all that have life.
9.9: All things which share in anything which is common to them all move towards that which is of the same kind as themselves. Everything which is earthy turns towards the earth, everything which is liquid flows together, and everything which is of an airy kind does the same, so that they need something to keep them apart, and the use of force. Fire indeed moves upwards on account of the elemental fire, but it is so ready to be kindled together with all the fire which is here that even every substance which is somewhat dry is easily set alight, because there is less mixed with it of what hinders burning. Accordingly, then, everything also which shares in the common intelligent nature moves in the same way towards what is of the same kind as itself, or moves even more. For the more superior it is in comparison with all other things, the more ready it also is to mingle and be fused with what is akin to it. Accordingly, among animals without reason we find swarms of bees, and herds of cattle, and the rearing of young birds, and in a way, loves; for even in animals there are souls, and the power which brings them together is seen to exert itself to a higher degree, and in such a way as has never been observed in plants or in stones or in trees. But in rational animals there are political communities and friendships, and families and gatherings of people; and in wars, treaties and truces. But in the things which are still higher, even though they are separated from one another, unity in a way exists, as in the stars. So the ascent to the higher degree is able to produce a sympathy even in things which are separated. See, then, what happens now; for only intelligent animals have now forgotten this mutual desire and inclination, and in them alone the property of flowing together is not seen. But still, though men try to avoid this union, they are caught and held by it, for their nature is too strong for them; and you will see what I mean, if you only observe. Sooner, then, will one find anything earthy which comes in contact with no earthy thing than a man completely separated from other men.
9.10: Man and God and the universe all produce fruit; each produces it at the proper seasons. But if usage has especially attached these terms to the vine and similar things, this is nothing. Reason produces fruit both for all and for itself, and from it are produced other things of the same kind as reason itself.
9.11: If you are able, correct by teaching those who do wrong; but if you cannot, remember that patience has been given to you for this purpose. And the gods too are patient with such people; and for some purposes they even help them to get health, wealth, reputation; so kind are they. And it is in your power too; or tell me, who stops you?
9.12: Do not labour as one who is wretched, nor as one who would be pitied or admired; but direct your will to one thing only—to set yourself in motion and to check yourself, as the social reason requires.
9.13: Today I have got out of all trouble, or rather I have thrown out all trouble, for it was not outside, but within and in my opinions.
9.14: All things are the same: familiar in experience, short-lived in time, and worthless in their matter. Everything now is just as it was in the time of those whom we have buried.
9.15: Things stand outside us, themselves by themselves, neither knowing anything of themselves nor expressing any judgement. What is it, then, which does judge them? The ruling faculty.
9.16: Not in passivity but in activity lie the evil and the good of the rational social animal, just as his virtue and his vice lie not in passivity but in activity.
9.17: For the stone which has been thrown up it is no evil to come down, nor indeed any good to have been carried up.
9.18: Look deep into men's leading principles, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what kind of judges they are of themselves.
9.19: All things are changing: and you yourself are in continuous change and in a way in continuous destruction, and the whole universe too.
9.20: It is your duty to leave another man's wrongful act where it is.
9.21: The ending of activity, the ceasing of movement and opinion, and in a sense their death, is no evil. Turn your thoughts now to your life: your life as a child, as a youth, your manhood, your old age, for in these too every change was a death. Is this anything to fear? Turn your thoughts now to your life under your grandfather, then to your life under your mother, then to your life under your father; and as you find many other differences and changes and endings, ask yourself: Is this anything to fear? In the same way, then, neither are the ending and ceasing and change of your whole life anything to be afraid of.
9.22: Hurry to examine your own ruling faculty and that of the universe and that of your neighbour: your own, so that you may make it just; that of the universe, so that you may remember what you are a part of; and that of your neighbour, so that you may know whether he has acted in ignorance or with knowledge, and may also consider that his ruling faculty is akin to yours.
9.23: As you yourself are a component part of a social system, so let every act of yours be a component part of social life. Whatever act of yours, then, has no reference, either directly or remotely, to a social end tears your life apart, and does not allow it to be one, and it is of the nature of a mutiny, just as when in a popular assembly a man acting by himself stands apart from the general agreement.
9.24: Quarrels of little children and their games, and poor spirits carrying about dead bodies—such is everything; and so what is shown in the representation of the dwellings of the dead strikes our eyes more clearly.
9.25: Examine the quality of the form of an object, and detach it completely from its material part, and then contemplate it; then determine the time, the longest which a thing of this particular form is naturally made to last.
9.26: You have endured endless troubles through not being content with your ruling faculty when it does the things which it is made by nature to do. But enough of this.
9.27: When another blames you or hates you, or when men say anything harmful about you, approach their poor souls, go deep within, and see what kind of men they are. You will discover that there is no reason to take any trouble that these men should have this or that opinion about you. However, you must be well disposed towards them, for by nature they are friends. And the gods too help them in every way, by dreams, by signs, towards gaining those things which they value.
9.28:
The cyclical movements of the universe are the same, up and down from age to age. And either the universal intelligence sets itself in motion for every separate effect, and if this is so, be content with what results from its activity; or it set itself in motion once, and everything else follows in a sort of sequence; or indivisible elements are the origin of all things.—In a word, if there is a god, all is well; and if chance rules, do not you too be governed by it.

Soon the earth will cover us all: then the earth too will change, and the things that result from change will also go on changing forever, and these again forever. For if a man reflects on the changes and transformations which follow one another like wave after wave, and on their speed, he will despise everything which is perishable.
9.29: The universal cause is like a winter torrent: it carries everything along with it. But how worthless are all these poor people who are engaged in political matters and, as they suppose, are playing the philosopher! All drivellers. Well then, man: do what nature now requires. Set yourself in motion, if it is in your power, and do not look about you to see if anyone will notice it; nor expect Plato's Republic: but be content if the smallest thing goes well, and consider such an outcome no small matter. For who can change men's opinions? And without a change of opinions, what else is there but the slavery of men who groan while they pretend to obey? Come now and tell me of Alexander and Philippus and Demetrius of Phalerum. They themselves shall judge whether they discovered what the common nature required, and trained themselves accordingly. But if they acted like tragic heroes, no one has condemned me to imitate them. Simple and modest is the work of philosophy. Do not draw me aside into insolence and pride.
9.30: Look down from above on the countless herds of men and their countless solemn ceremonies, and the endlessly varied voyages in storms and calms, and the differences among those who are born, who live together, and die. And consider, too, the life lived by others in olden times, and the life of those who will live after you, and the life now lived among barbarian nations, and how many do not even know your name, and how many will soon forget it, and how those who are perhaps praising you now will very soon blame you, and that neither a name after death is of any value, nor reputation, nor anything else.
9.31: Let there be freedom from disturbance with respect to the things which come from the external cause; and let there be justice in the things done by virtue of the internal cause, that is, let there be movement and action ending in this, in social acts, for this is in keeping with your nature.
9.32: You can remove from your way many useless things among those which disturb you, for they lie entirely in your opinion; and you will then gain ample space for yourself by grasping the whole universe in your mind, and by contemplating the eternity of time, and observing the rapid change of each separate thing, how short is the time from birth to dissolution, and the boundless time before birth as well as the equally boundless time after dissolution!
9.33: All that you see will quickly perish, and those who have watched its dissolution will very soon perish too. And he who dies in extreme old age will be brought into the same condition as he who died before his time.
9.34: What are these men's leading principles, and what kind of things are they busy about, and for what kind of reasons do they love and honour? Imagine that you see their poor souls laid bare. When they think that they do harm by their blame or good by their praise, what an idea!
9.35: Loss is nothing else than change. But the universal nature delights in change, and in obedience to her all things are now done well, and from eternity have been in the same form, and will be so for time without end. What, then, do you say—that all things have been and always will be bad, and that no power has ever been found among so many gods to set these things right, but the world has been condemned to be bound in never-ending evil?
9.36: The rottenness of the matter which is the foundation of everything! Water, dust, bones, filth: or again, marble rocks, the calluses of the earth; and gold and silver, the sediments; and clothes, only bits of hair; and purple dye, blood; and everything else is of the same kind. And that which is of the nature of breath is also another thing of the same kind, changing from this to that.
9.37: Enough of this wretched life and grumbling and monkey tricks. Why are you disturbed? What is new in this? What unsettles you? Is it the form of the thing? Look at it. Or is it the matter? Look at it. But besides these there is nothing. Towards the gods, then, now become at last simpler and better. It is the same whether we examine these things for a hundred years or three.
9.38: If a man has done wrong, the harm is his own. But perhaps he has not done wrong.
9.39: Either all things come from one intelligent source and come together as in one body, and the part ought not to find fault with what is done for the benefit of the whole; or there are only atoms, and nothing but mixture and dispersion. Why, then, are you disturbed? Say to the ruling faculty: Are you dead, are you corrupted, are you playing the hypocrite, have you become a beast, do you herd and feed with the rest?
9.40: Either the gods have no power or they have power. If, then, they have no power, why do you pray to them? But if they have power, why do you not pray for them to give you the ability not to fear any of the things which you fear, or not to desire any of the things which you desire, or not to be pained at anything, rather than pray that any of these things should not happen or should happen? For certainly if they can co-operate with men, they can co-operate for these purposes. But perhaps you will say the gods have placed them in your power. Well, then, is it not better to use what is in your power like a free man than to desire in a slavish and abject way what is not in your power? And who has told you that the gods do not help us even in the things which are in our power? Begin, then, to pray for such things, and you will see. One man prays like this: How shall I be able to lie with that woman? You pray like this: How shall I not desire to lie with her? Another prays like this: How shall I be released from this? You pray: How shall I not desire to be released? Another like this: How shall I not lose my little son? You like this: How shall I not be afraid to lose him? In short, turn your prayers this way, and see what comes of it.
9.41: Epicurus says: In my sickness my conversation was not about my bodily sufferings, nor, he says, did I talk on such subjects to those who visited me; but I continued to discuss the nature of things as before, keeping to this main point: how the mind, while sharing in such movements as go on in the poor flesh, may be free from disturbance and keep its proper good. Nor did I, he says, give the doctors a chance to put on solemn looks, as if they were doing something great, but my life went on well and happily. Do, then, the same as he did, both in sickness, if you are sick, and in any other circumstances; for never to abandon philosophy in whatever may happen to us, nor to engage in trifling talk with an ignorant man or with one unacquainted with nature, is a principle of all schools of philosophy; but to be intent only on what you are doing now and on the instrument by which you do it.
9.42: When you are offended by any man's shameless behaviour, immediately ask yourself: Is it possible, then, that there should be no shameless men in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, demand what is impossible. For this man too is one of those shameless men who must necessarily be in the world. Let the same thoughts be present to your mind in the case of the rogue, and the faithless man, and every man who does wrong in any way. For as soon as you remind yourself that it is impossible that such men should not exist, you will become more kindly disposed towards each one individually. It is useful to see this too, as soon as the occasion arises: what virtue nature has given to man to set against every wrongful act. For she has given to man, as an antidote against the stupid man, gentleness, and against another kind of man some other power. And in every case it is possible for you to correct, by teaching, the man who has gone astray; for every man who errs misses his aim and has gone astray. Besides, how have you been harmed? For you will find that none of those you are irritated with has done anything by which your mind could be made worse; and that which is evil and harmful to you has its foundation only in the mind. And what harm is done, or what is strange, if a man who has not been taught does the acts of an untaught man? Consider whether you should not rather blame yourself, because you did not expect such a man to err in such a way. For your reason gave you the means to suppose that he was likely to make this mistake, and yet you have forgotten, and are amazed that he has erred. But most of all, when you blame a man as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For the fault is clearly your own, whether you trusted that a man with such a disposition would keep his promise, or, when doing a kindness, you did not do it freely, nor in such a way as to have received all the benefit from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done a man a service? Are you not content that you have done something in keeping with your nature, and do you want to be paid for it? It is as if the eye demanded a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking. For just as these parts of the body are formed for a particular purpose, and by working according to their own makeup obtain what is their own, so too man is formed by nature for acts of kindness; and when he has done anything kind, or in any other way helpful to the common good, he has acted in keeping with his makeup, and he gets what is his own.
